findings.issue: `pendingLogin` is a single scalar string used to disable exactly one row's checkbox while its request is in flight (line 133: `disabled={pendingLogin === user.login}`). Because it can only hold one login at a time, toggling a second row while a first row's POST is still pending overwrites `pendingLogin` (line 70: `setPendingLogin(login)`), which silently re-enables the first row's checkbox even though its own request has not resolved yet.
findings.impact: An admin who toggles user A's checkbox and then, before the network round-trip completes, toggles user B's checkbox will see row A's checkbox become clickable again while A's original request is still outstanding. A follow-up click on A fires a second, overlapping `POST /api/v1/admin/users/A/access` with its own `granted` value. Because `setUsers` in the resolved handler (lines 74-78) applies whichever response lands last — not necessarily the one sent last — the checkbox the admin ends up seeing for row A can diverge from what was actually just persisted server-side, and the discrepancy is invisible until the next full page reload. This is a real, plausible sequence for the exact workflow this component exists for (an admin batch-granting/revoking several accounts in one sitting), not a contrived edge case.
findings.recommendation: Track pending state per row instead of a single value, e.g. `const [pendingLogins, setPendingLogins] = useState(() => new Set())`, add/remove `login` in that set around the request, and use `pendingLogins.has(user.login)` for `disabled`. This keeps every in-flight row correctly locked regardless of how many toggles are fired concurrently.

findings.issue: The `AdminUsersSection` function body spans lines 28-148 (121 lines), exceeding the project's >100-line function threshold.
findings.impact: Per the code-reviewing severity anchors, a function over 100 lines is a critical maintainability violation regardless of the language — it mixes state/effect wiring, the mount-fetch, the toggle handler, and the full row-rendering JSX (including the admin/non-admin checkbox branching and status-label logic) in one function, making it harder to reason about and to unit-test pieces independently in the future if test infra is ever added. Note in fairness: a large share of the length is JSX markup rather than branching business logic, so the practical complexity is lower than a 121-line imperative function would be — but the standard is stated as a line-count threshold, and this instance is a clean case of it.
findings.recommendation:
Extract the per-row rendering (the `
...
` block, roughly lines 110-142) into a small `UserRow` component that receives `user`, `isAdminRow`, `pendingLogin`/`pendingLogins`, and `onToggle` as props. That alone drops the parent function under 100 lines and gives each row's admin/non-admin branching a dedicated, independently readable unit.

findings.issue: `handleToggle` (lines 69-84) has no unmount guard, unlike the mount-fetch effect immediately above it (lines 38-65), which correctly uses a `cancelled` flag set in its cleanup function before calling any of the three `setUsers`/`setStatus`/`setNotice` setters. If an admin clicks a non-admin row's checkbox and then navigates to a different nav section (unmounting `AdminUsersSection`) before the `POST /api/v1/admin/users/{login}/access` promise settles, the `await` in `handleToggle` resolves after unmount and still calls `setUsers`, `setNotice`, or `setPendingLogin` on a component that is no longer mounted.
findings.impact: Produces the classic React 'Can't perform a state update on an unmounted component' warning and does wasted work updating state nobody will read — the exact class of bug the file's own mount-fetch effect was already written to avoid, just not carried over to the mutation path. It is inconsistent within the same file: one async operation is unmount-safe, the sibling one performing the state-changing side effect (the actual grant/revoke) is not.
findings.recommendation: Reuse the same `cancelled`/`isActive` pattern for the toggle: either lift a ref (e.g. `const isMountedRef = useRef(true)` set false in the fetch effect's cleanup) and check it before each setter inside `handleToggle`'s try/catch/finally, or restructure with an AbortController-style guard shared between the two effects/handlers.

summary: Functionally the component satisfies all four Task 8 acceptance criteria: admin rows are rendered checked+disabled with no onChange at all (the sole client-side guard against ever sending POST /api/v1/admin/users/{admin-login}/access, verified airtight — the admin branch's JSX literally never attaches a change handler, it isn't just disabled), non-admin toggles wire correctly to setUserAccess, the nav item and 'users' render branch are both gated on isAdmin derived from the row's own role field (not session-login comparison, as the spec required), and the non-optimistic update-from-request-value approach is correct given the server's confirmed 204 No Content response (server/internal/handler/access.go:162, handleSetAccess). All four self-disclosed deviations check out under independent verification: (1) the belt-and-suspenders isAdmin guard on the render branch is sound defensive coding matching the task's own reasoning; (2) the 204-body-less contract is confirmed against the actual handler and the update genuinely only happens after the request promise resolves, not before; (3) disabled-without-readOnly is confirmed via react-dom's own source (react-dom.development.js:1595) to suppress the controlled-checkbox-without-onChange warning, so no React warning would surface; (4) git diff -w confirms the Panel.jsx reindent carries no lost logic — only the isAdmin const, the third nav button, the three-way branch, and the panel-summary block relocation are real changes. Build is clean (npm run build with VITE_YA_CLIENT_ID=testclient). That said, the implementation has real defects: a concurrency gap where pendingLogin's single-value tracking lets one row's disabled-guard be defeated by toggling a different row mid-flight (enabling duplicate/overlapping POSTs and possible UI/server state drift), a missing unmount guard on the toggle handler that the sibling fetch effect already has, and a 121-line component function that breaches the project's >100-line severity anchor. None of these break the stated acceptance criteria outright, but they are genuine, fixable defects in newly written code, not nitpicks.
